Findings.Comment: The function signature accepts a context `ctx` and its documentation states it bounds the operation, but the diff replaces all uses with `context.Background()`. This ignores caller-provided cancellation, timeouts, and deadlines, which can cause unresponsive operations and resource leaks in applications that rely on context propagation for lifecycle management.

Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: The condition and assignment introduce an off-by-one that will cause a panic when a hunk is at the end of the file. For a slice of length L, the valid exclusive upper bound is L, not L+1. Setting `last = len(lines) + 1` when `last >= len(lines)` makes the subsequent `lines[first:last]` slice expression out of bounds when `first` is `len(lines)` (the hunk is at the end and context is requested).
Findings.Headline: Out-of-bounds slice access in ContextAfter

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The change replaces a `last > len(lines)` check with `last >= len(lines)` and sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`. This introduces an off-by-one error: when `first + n` exactly equals the slice length (i.e., the requested context reaches the end of the file), the new code sets `last` to an out-of-range index, causing `lines[first:last]` to panic. The original code set `last` to `len(lines)` to stop at the last line, which is correct. The change to `>=` is unnecessary and the assigned value is wrong.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one error in ContextAfter causes slice panic when context reaches end of file — blocking

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The condition `if last >= len(lines)` sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`, which will cause an out-of-bounds slice panic when calling `lines[first:last]` because `last` exceeds the slice length. For example, if `lines` has 10 items and `first` is 8 with `n` = 3, `last` becomes 11, then 12, and slicing `lines[8:12]` panics. The original condition `if last > len(lines)` with assignment `last = len(lines)` was correct, as it clips the slice to the end of the file.
Findings.Headline: Out-of-bounds slice panic in ContextAfter — blocking

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The boundary-clamping logic was changed from `last > len(lines)` / `last = len(lines)` to `last >= len(lines)` / `last = len(lines) + 1`. When `first + n` equals `len(lines)` (i.e., the hunk ends at the last line of the file and n equals the number of remaining lines), `last` is set to `len(lines) + 1`. The subsequent slice `lines[first:last]` then panics with an index-out-of-range because the maximum valid upper bound of a Go slice is `len(lines)`, not `len(lines) + 1`. Concrete example: `lines` has 10 elements, hunk `{Start:8, Count:2}`, `n=2` → `first=10`, `last=12`, clamped to `11`, slice `[10:11]` panics. The old code clamped to `10`, producing `[10:10]` which is a valid empty slice.
Findings.Headline: Out-of-bounds slice panic in ContextAfter — blocking

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: When `last` (first + n) is greater than or equal to `len(lines)`, the new code sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`. The slice operation `lines[first:last]` then uses an upper bound that is one beyond the slice length, causing a runtime panic. This occurs whenever the requested context runs to or past the end of the file.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one error in ContextAfter causes panic when context reaches end of file

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

While `q.pending` is read under the mutex in `Submit` and `Depth`, the `take` method is not shown, but the removal of the lock means concurrent calls to `Submit` can modify `q.pending` and `q.depth` while `worker` is reading `q.pending` and writing `q.depth` without synchronization, violating Go's memory model and causing undefined behavior.
Findings.Headline: Data race on queue depth and pending slice due to removed mutex

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The `worker` method updates `q.depth` without holding the mutex, while `Submit` and `Depth` both use the mutex when accessing `q.pending` and `q.depth`. This is a data race. Under concurrent access, the worker's update of `q.depth` may interleave with `Submit` or `Depth`, leading to an inconsistent view of the queue depth. Re-add the mutex lock and unlock around the update of `q.depth`.
Findings.Headline: Data race in worker's update of q.depth without mutex lock

This creates a data race: a concurrent `Submit` can change `q.pending` and `q.depth` while the worker is in the middle of `q.depth = len(q.pending)`, causing the depth to become inconsistent with the pending list.

This creates a data race: a concurrent call to `Submit` or `Depth` while the worker is writing to `depth` results in unsynchronized memory access, which is undefined behavior in Go and can cause crashes or corrupted reads.

Findings.Comment: The `tx.Commit(ctx)` error is ignored and the function returns `nil` even if the commit fails. This can lead the caller to believe the claim was added successfully when the transaction was actually rolled back by the deferred `tx.Rollback`. This is a data-loss risk because the caller might proceed as if the claim exists.
Findings.Headline: Commit error silently ignored in AddClaim — blocking

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The code now calls `tx.Commit(ctx)` without checking the returned error. If the commit fails (e.g., due to a deferred constraint violation or a transient database error), the function returns `nil` and the caller assumes success, while the data was not actually persisted. This is a data loss risk.
Findings.Headline: Commit error not handled in AddClaim

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

This misleads callers into believing the operation succeeded, leading to data inconsistency and silent failure. The commit error must be checked and returned to the caller.

Findings.Comment: The change swaps the error wrapping in the two error conditions. Now, when the database returns no row, the error wraps the raw `errNoRows` (instead of `ErrNoClaim`), and on other database errors it wraps `ErrNoClaim` (instead of the raw error). This breaks the function's contract: callers using `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` to detect no claim will now see `ErrNoClaim` on any database error and miss the no-claim case because the error no longer wraps `ErrNoClaim`.
Findings.Headline: Error wrapping swapped for no-row vs database errors

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
